title: Three Digits, One Picture
tagline: An hour, a page of random digits and a champion's three-digit syllables. How to pack even more into every picture.
card: A consonant, a vowel and a consonant: the three-digit system, and why champions build a thousand pictures.
goal: you will learn the consonant-vowel-consonant rule of the three-digit system, turn three digits into a syllable and a picture, and decode them back.

left_off.q: What is the 'room' of a date like 1492 in the timeline palace?
left_off.a: The fifteenth century: the century is carried by the place.

left_off.q: What does the ending 92 become in the Major System?
Why does the timeline palace keep events in order?
left_off.a: The walk from room to room goes from the oldest century to the newest.

text: In a large hall, a competitor sits in front of a sheet of paper covered in rows of random digits. There are no words, no names, no dates: just 7, 3, 9, 1, 0, 4, 2, and thousands more. The rule is simple. You have one hour to learn as many as you can, and then you must write them back in order.

This is one of the long events at a memory championship. The best competitors in the world learn thousands of digits in an hour, and then recall them with only a few mistakes. For this event, one picture for every two digits is too slow. They need a picture for every three.

check.q: What is the task in the hour event?
check.a: Learn as many random digits as possible in an hour, then write them back in order.

parts.talk: How many digits do you think a person could learn in an hour? What would the limit be?

text: A British memory athlete, Ben Pridmore, who won the world title several times in the 2000s, is the person after whom a three-digit system is named. The idea is natural: if two digits can be one picture, three can be one picture too. The cost is size: instead of 100 pictures, you need a thousand, one for every number from 000 to 999.

To build a thousand pictures you need a rule that makes them quickly. The rule is the syllable. A syllable has a start, a middle and an end. Three digits: three sounds. That is the key to the whole system.

check.q: How many pictures does a three-digit system need?
check.a: A thousand: one for each of 000 to 999.

parts.talk: Would you be willing to learn a thousand pictures to be able to memorise faster? What would you use it for?

text: The cost is not as high as it sounds. You will not build the thousand in a week. Most people start with a hundred and add a hundred at a time. And the pictures are not random: they come from a rule, and the rule gives you a word or a name or a sound-alike for every number.

In this lesson you learn the rule. The first digit gives a consonant, the second a vowel, the third another consonant, and the three together give a syllable. A syllable is a word, or close enough to one to make a picture.

check.q: What does the rule give you for each three-digit number?
check.a: A syllable: a consonant, a vowel and a consonant, which gives a word or something close to one.

parts.talk: How would you make a picture for a syllable that is not a real word?

words.m: a unit of sound in a word. Cat has one syllable; table has two.
a person who takes part in a competition.
to fit a lot into a small space. Pack more into each picture.
a statement of how something must be done.

source: The three-digit system is named after the British memory competitor Ben Pridmore. Vowel assignments differ from one person to another; the table below is one that works and is used in this course.

method.x: Take three digits. The first and the third become consonants (from the Major System). The middle one becomes a vowel sound (from a table). The result is a syllable.

items.x: m + ee + n = MEAN. Picture someone mean: scowling, shouting.

method.x: When the syllable is not a word
Some syllables are not words. 823 = f + e + m = fem? Use a similar-sounding word (fan), a name (Fenn), or an abbreviation. The picture must be one you can see and always the same.

method.x: The two are often combined: PAO for cards, and a three-digit system for digits. Both rely on the Major System, which you already have.
Turn 372, 914 and 541 into words aloud, using the tables, and say the picture for each.

try.title: Decode these words
try.prompt: Each word is a three-digit number. Match them.

items.s: 322: m + ___ + n, which makes the word MEN.
360: m + ___ + z, which makes MAZE (the middle sound is 'ay').

try.title: Encode 510 and 244
try.prompt: 510 = l + a + s (LASS or LACE). 244 = n + o + r (NOR or NO?). Pick a word or sound-alike for each and make a picture.
try.model: 510: a girl (lass) is wearing a dress made of lace, with a long white veil. 244: a big sign says NOR in lights over a Viking (a Norse man) marching in.
checks: They are different from each other.

try.title: A syllable that is not a word
try.prompt: 823 = f + e + m. There is no obvious word. Decide on a word or a name or a sound-alike, and make a picture.
try.model: FEM sounds like 'fan'. A giant red fan blows a dancer's skirt up and down the stage. (Or use a name: Fenn.)
checks: I found a sound-alike or name.
I will always use the same one for 823.

try.title: Six digits, two pictures
try.prompt: Encode 372914 as two pictures: 372 and 914. Put them in two places of a route.
try.model: 372 MEAN: a scowling man shakes his fist at the front door. 914 PAR: a golf ball sits in the hall, rolling into a cup. Two places, six digits.
checks: Each is in its own place.

try.q: How many pictures does the three-digit system need?
try.why: One for each of the numbers 000 to 999.

try.title: Say the rule
try.prompt: Explain the rule to an imaginary friend in one minute: what each of the three digits gives, and an example.

cards: A vowel from the table: 0 oo, 1 a, 2 e, 3 i, 4 o, 5 u, 6 ay, 7 ee, 8 igh, 9 oh.
Use a sound-alike, a name, or an abbreviation, and always the same one.

quiz.q: What number is the word BAG?
What does the middle digit give?
quiz.why: A vowel sound from the table.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: six syllables
challenge.intro: These six words stand for 372 914 541 133 107 360. Learn them in order as one story, then type them back. Afterwards decode them into digits.
challenge.study: A mean man; a golf par; a car park; Tim; someone took something; a maze.

look_back.q: In the timeline palace, what does the room carry and what does the picture carry?
look_back.a: The room carries the century; the picture carries the last two digits.

look_back.q: How many digits does one PAO scene hold?
What sound is 5 in the Major System?

look_back.a: A place on a palace route where a picture sits.
